code.title: Toy next-word predictor: an LLM in miniature

followUps:
It is bad at anything that needs exact facts it was never given, exact arithmetic, and knowing what is true today.

It writes likely-sounding text, so it can invent a policy number or a court case with full confidence. It also cannot see your database, and it forgets everything between calls. Fixes: give it the facts in the prompt (retrieval), let it call a calculator or API (tools), and check outputs in code. Example: asked for the total of 37 invoices, it may be off by a few; a tool call summing the numbers is exact.

A search engine finds and returns existing documents; an LLM writes new text that sounds right.

Search gives you a source you can click and check. An LLM gives you a fluent answer that may blend several things it learned and may have no source at all. They work well together: search (or vector search) finds the right pages, and the LLM reads them and writes a short answer with references. That pattern is called RAG. Use search when you need the original document, an LLM when you need it summarised or reshaped.

code.title: Estimate tokens and cost before a call

followUps:
Code has many symbols, brackets, indentation and unusual names, and those split into more small pieces than ordinary words do.

A common English word like "table" is often one token. A name like GetCustomerOrderHistoryAsync may be five or six, and every {, ; and run of spaces counts. So 100 words of prose might be 130 tokens while 100 words of dense code might be 200 or more. It matters for cost and for the context window when you paste source files.

Use the provider's token counting endpoint or tokenizer library for the exact number; use characters divided by 4 for a quick estimate.

Each model family has its own tokenizer, so a count from one model is only close for another. Many APIs also return the real input and output token counts in the response, which is the best data for cost tracking. Before sending, an estimate is enough to decide whether to trim: for example 40,000 characters is about 10,000 tokens. Leave room for the reply.

code.title: Check that a request fits in the context window

followUps:
No. The context window is the total space for input and output together; the output limit is a separate, smaller cap on just the reply.

For example a model may accept 200,000 tokens in total but allow only 8,000 tokens of reply. Your input plus the reply must fit in the window, and the reply must also stay under the output cap. If you send 195,000 tokens in, only about 5,000 are left for the answer. Always reserve room for the reply when you trim.

Because a bigger prompt costs more, is slower, and often gives worse answers, since the useful sentence is buried among many irrelevant ones.

Pasting a 300-page manual to answer a one-line question wastes about 150,000 tokens per call. At 1,000 calls a day that is a large bill and several seconds of extra delay. Better: find the 3 to 5 relevant passages with search and send only those, about 2,000 tokens. Long inputs also risk hitting the window limit.

code.title: Temperature reshapes next-token probabilities

followUps:
Not always. At temperature 0 you get the most likely token each time, but results can still differ slightly between calls.

Reasons include floating-point differences when many requests are batched on the GPU, ties between equally likely tokens, and the provider updating the model behind the same name. So do not build logic that needs byte-identical replies. For stable behaviour, cache the answer you accepted, validate the output in code, and test with an evaluation set rather than one example.

Top-p (nucleus sampling) limits the model to the smallest group of top tokens whose probabilities add up to p, then picks among them.

With top-p 0.9, if the best tokens have chances 0.6, 0.2, 0.1 and then a long tail, the first three already add to 0.9, so only those three are possible and the tail is cut off. It is another way to control randomness. Usually change either temperature or top-p, not both. Some newer models fix these settings and ignore them.

code.title: Grounding check: is every claim in the sources?

followUps:
No. You can reduce hallucinations a lot, but you cannot guarantee zero, because the model is always choosing likely text.

So design for it: ground answers in retrieved sources, ask for citations, say "I don't know" when sources are empty, validate outputs in code (ids exist, numbers match), and keep a human in the loop for high-risk actions. State a target such as "fewer than 2% unsupported answers on our test set", not "never".

Build a test set of real questions with known good answers, run the system, and count the answers that contain claims not supported by the sources.

Example: 200 questions, a reviewer (or a judge model checked against humans) marks each answer supported or not; 6 unsupported means a 3% rate. Track it for each prompt or model change. Sample live traffic too, because real users ask things your test set missed.

code.title: Stateless model: the app resends the history

followUps:
Store it in your own database (SQL Server, Cosmos DB or Postgres) keyed by conversation id, and load the recent turns for each request.

A simple table: Messages(ConversationId, Seq, Role, Content, Tokens, CreatedAt) plus an owner user id for access checks. For short-lived chats a distributed cache such as Redis with an expiry is fine. Do not keep it only in server memory: with two instances or a restart the chat is lost. Never trust a history sent back by the browser without checking it.

Save the useful facts from each conversation in a store, and load the relevant ones into the prompt at the start of the next session.

Steps: at the end of a chat (or as it goes) extract stable facts such as "prefers metric units" with a model call, store them per user with a timestamp, and retrieve them by relevance when a new chat starts. Let users view and delete memories, because it is personal data. Keep it small: 10 short facts cost far less than replaying old chats.

code.title: Sliding window: keep the system prompt and the last N turns

followUps:
Early facts that the user stated once: names, ids, constraints, and decisions that were made.

Summaries keep the topic but drop precise details such as "order 1042", a date, a number, or a "never do X" rule. A fix is to pull such facts into a separate pinned section ("Known facts: order 1042, deadline 5 May") that is always sent, and to tell the summariser to keep ids, numbers, names and open questions.

Replay long saved conversations through the trimming logic and check that questions that depend on early facts are still answered correctly.

Example test: turn 2 says "my order is 1042"; after 30 filler turns and trimming, ask "what was my order number?". Score the answer against the expected one. Run a set of such cases for every change to the window size or summary prompt, and report the pass rate.

code.title: Pick the cheapest model that passes our quality bar

followUps:
When data cannot leave your network, when volume is so high that per-token prices lose to your own GPU costs, or when you need to customise the model deeply.

The price is real work: GPUs, scaling, patching, monitoring and your own safety layer. A common rule: use a hosted API until the monthly bill or a compliance rule clearly justifies a team to run models. Check the open-weight model's licence too, and test it on your own evaluation set first.

Treat it like a dependency end-of-life: track the dates, test the replacement early, and switch behind configuration.

Keep the model name in config, not in code. When a retirement notice arrives (often months ahead), run your evaluation set on the new version, fix prompt differences, roll out to 5% of traffic, then 100%, with the old one as a quick rollback until its retirement date. Alerts on the retirement calendar stop surprises.

Put the model name, max output tokens, timeout and maybe temperature in configuration (appsettings or your config service), so you can change them without a release.

Do not let end users set them. Keep the system prompt and safety limits in versioned code or a controlled store. Per-environment overrides are useful: a cheap model in development, the real one in production. Hard-code nothing that you may need to change during an incident.

Small language models are good for narrow, high-volume tasks: classifying tickets, extracting fields, routing, and short rewrites.

They are cheaper and faster, and can run on your own hardware or a laptop, which helps with privacy. They are weaker at long reasoning and broad knowledge. A common design is a small model for easy cases and a larger one for hard cases, with a measured pass rate on each tier.

code.title: Keep system rules and user text in separate messages

followUps:
Assume yes. Users can often trick a model into repeating its instructions, so treat the system prompt as readable.

Do not put secrets, keys, internal URLs or private business rules in it. Enforce real rules (who may see what) in code, not by asking the model to keep a secret. It is fine for the prompt to hold tone and format rules; if a competitor read it, nothing important should leak.

In source control next to the code, as template files or resources, with a version id that is logged on every call.

Example: Prompts/support.v3.txt embedded in the assembly, loaded through a small IPromptProvider. Changes go through a pull request, run against the evaluation set, and deploy like any release. A database or config store makes sense only if you need changes without a deploy, and then keep history and an approval step.

code.title: Build a prompt from task, context and format parts

followUps:
Say exactly what the reply may contain and what it must not, and use structured output when you can.

Add lines like "Reply with the three bullets only, no introduction and no closing remark". Showing one example of the exact shape helps. For machine use, request JSON with a schema so there is no room for chat text, and parse only that. As a last step, strip or reject anything outside the expected format in code.

Vague prompts: no audience, no format, no example, and no instruction for what to do when the answer is unknown.

"Summarise this" leaves length, tone and focus to chance, so the answer changes each time. A second common mistake is changing the prompt without testing it on saved examples, so one fix quietly breaks another case. Be specific and keep a test set.

code.title: Build a few-shot prompt from labelled examples

followUps:
Chain-of-thought prompting asks the model to work through the steps before giving the final answer, which helps on multi-step problems.

Example: "A pack has 12 items; a box holds 5 packs; how many items in 3 boxes?" The model writes 12 x 5 = 60, then 60 x 3 = 180. Many newer models reason internally, so you often just select a reasoning setting instead. It costs extra output tokens, so use it only where plain answers are wrong.

Pick examples that are clear, cover each category and the tricky edge cases, and look exactly like real inputs.

Use 3 to 8 examples, balanced across labels (not five BILLING and one BUG), and in mixed order so the model does not just copy the last one. Test the set on your evaluation data and swap examples that cause errors. Never use an example that contains private customer data.

code.title: Validate model JSON and retry once on failure

followUps:
Retry once with the error message added to the prompt; if it still fails, return a safe fallback and log it.

Steps: parse and validate; on failure send the original request plus "Your reply failed validation: category must be one of BILLING, DELIVERY, BUG". Limit to 1 or 2 retries so cost stays bounded. Final fallback: route to a human or a default category. Count the failure rate; a rising rate means the prompt or model changed.

An enum limits the model to your allowed values, so your code can switch on it safely without handling free text like "billing issue?" or "Billing".

With a schema enum of ["BILLING","DELIVERY","BUG","OTHER"] the output is one of four known strings, and you map it to a C# enum. Always include an OTHER or UNKNOWN value so the model has an honest option instead of forcing a wrong label.

code.title: Versioned prompt templates with named placeholders

followUps:
They can propose and test wording, but changes should still go through version control, review and the evaluation set before reaching production.

A practical setup: PMs edit a prompt file through a pull request template or a small internal tool that opens a PR. The pipeline runs the evals and shows the pass rate on the PR. That gives them speed without risk of an untested edit breaking a live feature.

Send a share of traffic to each version, log the version id, and compare outcome metrics after enough requests.

Example: 10% of users get v2. Compare thumbs-up rate, task completion, escalation to human, token cost and latency. Use the offline evaluation set first, so the live test is only for versions that already pass. Assign users, not single requests, to a variant so each person has a consistent experience.

Fine-tuning bakes knowledge into the model weights at training time, so every change in a fact means training again; retrieval just reads the latest document.

If your price list changes weekly, a fine-tuned model keeps quoting last month's prices and you cannot show where an answer came from or delete one document. With RAG you re-index the changed file in minutes. Fine-tuning is better for style, format and behaviour that stays stable.

Hundreds to thousands of high-quality example pairs (input and the ideal output), consistent, reviewed, and representative of real traffic.

Bad or inconsistent examples teach bad habits. Keep a separate held-out set (for example 10%) to measure the result, and remove personal data. Before collecting data, check that a better prompt with a few examples does not already reach your quality bar; it usually costs far less.

code.title: Prompt caching only matches a shared prefix

followUps:
A cached full answer may be shown to the wrong user or be out of date, so it must be keyed by everything that affects the answer.

If two users ask "what is my balance?" and you cache by the question text, the second user sees the first user's balance. Key by tenant, user permissions, prompt version and data version, give it a short expiry, and avoid caching answers that include personal data.

Watch the cached-token count the API returns; a sudden drop to zero, plus a rise in cost and latency, means the prefix changed.

Typical causes: a timestamp, request id or user name moved to the top of the prompt, tool definitions listed in a different order, or a small edit to the system text. Log cached versus uncached input tokens per request and alert when the cache-hit share falls below its usual level (for example from 80% to 5%).

code.title: Embeddings: similar meaning, similar numbers

followUps:
No. Vectors from different models live in different spaces, so their numbers and even their lengths mean different things.

Similarity between a model-A vector and a model-B vector is meaningless. The query and the stored documents must use the same model and version. If you change the model, you must re-embed everything, which is why teams store the model name next to each vector.

Images, audio, code, products and users can all be embedded, as long as a model exists for that type.

Examples: search photos by a text description with a text-and-image model, find similar code snippets, or recommend products with similar descriptions. Multimodal models put text and images in the same space so one query can match both. Your vector store does not care what the numbers came from.

code.title: Vector search: brute-force top-k nearest

followUps:
Keyword search wins when the user types an exact thing: an error code, a product SKU, a name, or a rare technical term.

A query like "ERR_4021" or "invoice INV-88231" has no meaning to spread; the exact string is what matters, and vectors may return similar-looking but wrong codes. That is why many systems use hybrid search, combining both.

Store the source document id, title, section heading, URL, date, language, tenant id, and access groups.

This lets you cite sources, filter by tenant and permission before ranking, prefer fresh documents, delete or update by document id, and debug a bad result. Also store the embedding model name and chunk position, and a content hash to detect unchanged files.

code.title: Tiny RAG: retrieve the best passage, then build the prompt

followUps:
Usually retrieval returned the wrong or incomplete passages, so the model had nothing correct to work from.

The cause is often upstream: poor chunking, a PDF table parsed into garbage, an outdated document, or a query that needs different words. Look at the retrieved chunks first. If the right text is in them and the answer is still wrong, then it is a prompt or model problem.

RAG is the wrong tool when the data is small enough to paste, when you need exact calculations or database queries, or when the task is about style rather than knowledge.

For "total sales in March" use a SQL query through a tool; searching text chunks will give a guess. For a 2-page policy, just include it in the prompt. RAG also adds ingestion, an index and permission handling, so do not add it without a clear need.

Measure retrieval first: for each test question, is the right passage in the top results?

If retrieval misses, nothing later can fix it, and it is cheap to test without calling a model. Metric example: recall at 5 (the share of questions whose correct chunk appears in the top 5). Say 42 of 50 questions hit, so recall@5 is 84%. Then measure answer quality using the retrieved text.

Rewrite the follow-up into a standalone question using the chat history, then search with that.

User: "What is the refund window?" then "And for sale items?" The second alone searches badly. A short model call turns it into "What is the refund window for sale items?", which retrieves the right passage. Send the original conversation turns to the final answer call so the tone is natural.

code.title: Chunk text into overlapping windows of words

followUps:
Do not chunk it by size; turn each row (or small group of related rows) into its own chunk that repeats the column names and the table title.

Example chunk: "Pricing table, Pro plan: seats 10, price 49 EUR per month, support: email." Cutting a table in the middle separates numbers from their headers. For heavy numeric lookups, store the table in a database and let the model query it through a tool.

You search small chunks for precision, but send the larger parent section to the model for context.

Each small chunk (say 150 tokens) stores the id of its parent (a 800-token section). When a small chunk matches, you fetch its parent and send that. It fixes the small-versus-large trade-off: exact matching plus enough surrounding text. Remove duplicates when two hits share a parent.

code.title: Cosine, dot product and distance on unit vectors

followUps:
Exact search is good enough up to roughly tens of thousands of vectors, or even a few hundred thousand when a query can take 50 to 100 ms.

Comparing a query with 50,000 vectors of 1,000 numbers is 50 million multiplications, which a modern CPU does in milliseconds. At millions of vectors, or when many queries run each second, use an approximate index. Exact search is also useful as the reference to measure the approximate one.

Run both on the same queries and see what share of the true top-k the approximate index returns.

For 1,000 test queries compute the exact top-10 by brute force. If the approximate index returns on average 9.6 of those 10, recall@10 is 96%. Tune index settings (search breadth) until recall meets your target at an acceptable latency.

code.title: Reciprocal rank fusion merges two ranked lists

followUps:
Reciprocal rank fusion gives each document a score of 1/(k + rank) in every list and adds the scores, so items that rank high in several lists rise to the top.

It needs no score scaling between keyword and vector search, since only positions are used. A document ranked 1st and 3rd scores about 1/61 + 1/63 = 0.0323, beating one that is 1st in only one list (0.0164).

Usually 3 to 8 passages after reranking, as few as still contain the answer.

More chunks means more cost, more delay and more distracting text, and models can miss details in the middle of long context. Start from 5, test on your evaluation set with 3, 5 and 8, and pick the smallest number where answer quality stops improving.

Track retrieval recall on a test set, share of answers with citations, share of "I don't know" replies, user thumbs, latency and cost per question.

Also show index freshness (age of the newest document) and the ingestion failure count. Example panel: recall@5 84%, unsupported answers 3%, p95 latency 4.2 s, 12 failed documents. Alert on drops after a deploy or a data load.

Do not let the model silently choose; prefer the newer or more authoritative source by metadata, and show both when you cannot tell.

Store effective date and source ranking with every chunk, filter out superseded versions at ingestion, and tell the model in the prompt: "If sources disagree, say so and cite both, preferring the later date". Report unresolved conflicts to the content owner.

code.title: Apply the permission filter before ranking

followUps:
Keep permission checks live at query time, with short caches, so a revoked right takes effect within seconds, and remove the user from the groups used in the filter.

The filter reads current group membership (cached for maybe 1 to 5 minutes) instead of values copied into the index at ingestion. If the chunk's own access list changes, update its metadata through an event. For urgent revocations, also invalidate the user's session and cached answers.

Use one shared index with a mandatory tenant filter for most cases; use one index per tenant when contracts, size or isolation rules demand it.

Shared index: cheaper, easier to run, but one missing filter leaks data, so enforce the filter in a single data-access layer and test it. Per-tenant index: strong isolation and easy deletion, but cost and operations grow with every customer. A mix is common: shared for small tenants, separate for large or regulated ones.

Build the new index beside the old one, fill it in the background, test it, then switch the query side to it and drop the old one.

Steps: create index v2 with the new model, re-embed all documents (new ones go to both during the copy), run the evaluation set on v2 and compare recall, then change a config flag to read from v2, with v1 kept for a few days as a rollback. Never mix vectors from two models in one index.

Measure first, but usually start with ingestion cost and retrieval quality; these affect all later numbers.

Typical wins in order: skip unchanged documents by content hash, batch embedding calls, add a metadata pre-filter so searches scan less, reduce chunks sent to the model with reranking, and use a smaller model for easy questions. Use per-stage timings and cost dashboards to find the real biggest piece.

A semantic cache can return one user's answer to another user who asked something similar, bypassing permissions and personal context.

"What is my leave balance?" from two people is the same meaning but different correct answers. Only cache questions whose answers do not depend on the user, partition the cache by tenant and permission set, add short expiry, and keep a high similarity threshold.

Choose k by testing: start at 5, compare quality and cost at several values using your evaluation set.

Too small a k misses the answer when the best chunk is ranked 6th; too large adds noise and cost. If the correct chunk is nearly always in the top 4 but sometimes 9th, retrieve 20, rerank and send the best 4 to the model.

code.title: The app, not the model, runs the tool

followUps:
It reads the names and descriptions you gave for each tool, and picks the one whose description matches the user's need.

So the description is the most important part: "Gets the shipping status of one order by numeric id. Use when the user asks where their order is" works better than "order tool". Keep the list short (a handful of tools is better than fifty), make names distinct, and test with questions that should and should not call a tool.

Your app should catch it and send an error result back, such as "unknown tool", without running anything.

Look the name up in your own registry of allowed tools; if it is missing, return a message listing the valid tools so the model can correct itself, and log it. Never build a call from a model-supplied name by reflection or a dynamic lookup that could reach other methods.

code.title: One tool call, message by message

followUps:
Return a short, clear error message as the tool result, and let the model decide how to continue; never crash the whole chat.

Example result: {"error":"Order service timed out, try again later"}. The model can then apologise or retry. Do not include stack traces, connection strings or internal paths. Log the full exception on your side with the trace id.

The id links each result to the exact request it answers, which matters when the model asks for several tools at once.

If the model requests GetOrderStatus for 1042 and GetOrderStatus for 1043 in the same turn, your results may come back in a different order. With ids call_1 and call_2 the model knows which result belongs to which order. It also helps logging and replay.

code.title: Agent loop with a step limit

followUps:
A good fit is an open-ended task where the steps depend on what is found, such as investigating a failed deployment.

The agent reads logs, finds an error, checks the recent change, looks at configuration, and suggests a fix; the number and order of steps cannot be planned in advance. Keep it read-only, limit its steps, and let a human approve any change.

It stops when the model replies with a final answer instead of another tool call, but you must also add your own limits.

Set a maximum number of steps (for example 10), a time budget, and a token or cost budget. If any limit is reached, stop and return what was found or escalate. Also stop when it repeats the same tool call with the same arguments, which is a sign of a loop.

Function calling is the model's ability to request a function; MCP is a standard way to discover and connect many tools to many AI applications.

With plain function calling you define tools inside each app and for each provider. With MCP a tool server publishes its tools once, and any MCP-capable client can list and call them. MCP uses function calling underneath: the client turns MCP tools into the tool definitions the model sees.

Treat it as an API: authenticate every caller, authorise per user, validate every argument, and log all calls.

Use HTTPS and OAuth tokens (for example from Microsoft Entra ID) with narrow scopes, never a shared static key. Pass the end user's identity so the server checks their rights. Only connect servers you trust, since tool descriptions are text the model reads and can carry hidden instructions. Rate limit and audit.

code.title: Validate arguments and authorize inside the tool

followUps:
Because one tool that runs any SQL lets a single bad or injected instruction read or change everything the database account can reach.

A prompt injection could produce DROP TABLE or SELECT * FROM Users. Prefer narrow tools such as GetOrdersForCurrentUser(from, to) with parameterised queries. If you need free-form queries, use a read-only account, a restricted view, row-level security, a timeout and a row limit.

From the validated sign-in token of the request your API received, which your code puts into the tool context; never from the model's arguments.

In ASP.NET Core read it from HttpContext.User (the oid or sub claim, plus tenant and roles) and pass it to the tool implementation. The model can only choose arguments such as an order id; your code checks that this user may see it.

code.title: Why long agent runs fail: errors compound

followUps:
Evaluate the whole run: did it reach the right end result, how many steps and tokens did it use, and did it avoid forbidden actions?

Create test tasks with a known good outcome (for example "ticket 88 must end up tagged BILLING and assigned to team X"), run each several times, and record success rate, steps, cost, and tool errors. Also check the path for unsafe calls. Single-answer scoring misses loops and wasted work.

Multiple agents pay off when sub-tasks are independent and large, need different tools or context, and can run in parallel.

Example: one agent reads 50 contracts in parallel (each with its own context) and a lead agent merges the summaries. For small tasks a single agent with tools is simpler, cheaper and easier to debug. Each extra agent adds cost, delay and more ways to fail.

code.title: Test properties of an AI answer, not exact text

followUps:
Start with 30 to 50 realistic examples; grow to a few hundred as you find failures.

That is enough to catch big regressions after a change. Include normal cases, edge cases, known past failures and abuse attempts. Every bug a user reports becomes a new test. For small differences between versions you need more examples, because 2 extra passes out of 40 may just be noise.

It depends on the risk: set the bar from the cost of a wrong answer, agree it before testing, and use a stricter gate for safety checks.

A draft-email helper might ship at 85% good with human edit. A refund tool may need 99% and a human approval step. Safety tests such as "never reveals another user's data" should be 100%. Also compare against the current baseline: it must not be worse than what users have now.

code.title: Score an evaluation set and compare two prompts

followUps:
Compare the judge's scores with human scores on a sample of answers; if they agree most of the time, the judge is usable.

Have two people grade 50 answers, then run the judge on the same 50. If the judge agrees with the humans on 45 (90%) and the humans agree with each other about as often, it is reliable enough. Use a clear rubric, ask for a short reason, and re-check periodically because judge models change.

Add new cases from live failures, and remove or update cases that no longer reflect the product or the real questions.

Every month sample recent traffic, add the cases where users complained or the answer was wrong, and retire cases about discontinued features. Keep a stable core set so scores stay comparable over time. Version the set so you know which one produced a given number.

code.title: Estimate monthly cost from tokens

followUps:
You need the number of chats per user, turns per chat, average input and output tokens per call, and the price per million tokens of each kind.

Example: 10,000 users x 8 chats x 6 turns = 480,000 calls. At 1,500 input and 300 output tokens, that is 720M input and 144M output tokens a month; with placeholder prices of 3 and 15 dollars per million that is 2,160 + 2,160 = about 4,300 dollars. Also ask about caching, retries and peak usage.

Log the tenant id with the token counts of every call, then multiply by price and sum per tenant.

Put the tenant and feature name into your logging or metrics (and, if the provider supports it, into request tags). Store usage in a table or telemetry store so finance can see cost per tenant per month. Include shared costs such as embedding and indexing, split by usage or document count.

code.title: Latency = first token + output length / speed

followUps:
Input is processed in parallel in one fast pass, but output tokens are produced one after another, each waiting for the previous one.

Sending 1,000 more input tokens might add 0.1 seconds. Asking for 1,000 more output tokens at about 50 tokens per second adds about 20 seconds. So ask for short answers, avoid long reasoning when not needed, and stream the reply.

Base it on how people use it: time to first token under about 1 to 2 seconds, and total time that matches the task, measured at the 95th percentile.

For a chat: first text within 1.5 s for 95% of requests, finished within 15 s. For a nightly batch job, minutes are fine. Measure real traffic, set the target per feature, and alert when it is missed.

Use a cheap first check: simple requests are short, match known intents, need no tools, and a small model passes your evaluation set on them.

Build a router: a rules step or a small classifier labels each request, simple ones go to the small model, the rest to the big one. Validate by running the evaluation set for each tier; if the small model passes 95% of the "simple" group at one-fifth of the cost, route them there. Sample routed traffic regularly.

A cache can return a stale or wrong-user answer, so key it carefully and expire it.

Key by the full question plus tenant, permissions, prompt version and data version. Do not cache answers with personal data unless the key includes the user. Keep expiry short for facts that change. A semantic cache adds the risk of matching a different question with a similar meaning, so use a high threshold.

Find the request by trace id, then look at the prompt version, retrieved chunks, tool calls and the model reply to see which stage went wrong.

If the chunks are wrong it is retrieval; if they are right and the answer is wrong it is the prompt or model; if a tool returned an error it is the tool. Add the case to your evaluation set, fix, and re-run. Redact personal data in logs and limit who can read them.

Show request volume, cost per day and per tenant, p50 and p95 latency, error and throttle (429) rate, cache-hit rate, thumbs-down rate, and evaluation pass rate.

Add model and prompt version annotations on the chart so a change is visible. Example alerts: cost per day above 150% of average, p95 above target, 429s above 2%. Keep one page that a new team member can understand.

Not automatically; look at how much the weaker category matters, and fix or accept it with eyes open.

If the drop is in a low-risk category (say 91% to 88% on small talk) and the gain elsewhere is large, ship with a rollback plan. If it is a critical one (refund decisions), try prompt changes first or keep routing that category to the old model until retirement. Decide with numbers from the evaluation set and write down the trade-off.

Run the new model after the user's answer is already sent, in the background or from a queue, and only record its output for comparison.

The user sees the old model's reply on time. A background job (or a copy of the request on a worker) calls the new model, stores both replies, and a script compares them. It doubles model cost for the sampled share, so sample 5 to 10 percent of traffic.

A jailbreak is a prompt that tries to make the model break its own safety rules; prompt injection tries to make it follow the attacker's instructions instead of the application's.

They overlap: both are attacks through text. Jailbreaks target the model's built-in limits (say, writing harmful content). Injection targets your app's behaviour (leak data, call a tool). Both are handled with layers, not one filter.

Because language has endless ways to say the same thing, so a list of bad phrases always misses some variants, and also blocks innocent users.

An attacker can rephrase, use another language, split words, encode in base64 or hide text in a document. A filter of "ignore previous instructions" is easily bypassed. It can be a cheap extra layer, but real protection comes from limiting what the model can do.

code.title: Least privilege: approval gate for risky tools

followUps:
Because the model treats instructions as text to weigh, not as rules it must obey, and a clever attacker's text can outweigh yours.

Your sentence "ignore malicious instructions" is just more text next to the attacker's text. It lowers the success rate but cannot prove safety. So you also limit what the model can do: narrow tools, user-level permissions, output checks and human approval for risky actions.

Build a set of attack prompts and poisoned documents, run them against the feature automatically, and check that no forbidden tool call, data leak or rule break happens.

Include direct attacks, hidden instructions in web pages and files, and multi-turn tricks. Add each new attack found to the suite and run it on every change. Also do manual red-team sessions, since people invent new tricks.

code.title: Mask personal data before it leaves your system

followUps:
Act quickly and calmly: stop the leak, report it to security and the data protection contact, and follow the incident process.

Find out what was pasted and by whom, whether it was personal or secret data, and what the tool's terms say. Rotate any exposed secrets. Do not blame the person: explain the approved tool and the rule, and add technical controls such as a company AI account and data-loss prevention.

Insist on self-hosting when the data may not leave your network by law or contract, or when you need full control over where processing happens.

Examples: certain government, defence or health data. Before deciding, check whether a regional cloud deployment, a private endpoint, or zero data retention terms already meet the rule, since self-hosting means you run GPUs, updates and safety yourself.

code.title: Treat model output as untrusted: encode and validate

followUps:
If your page inserts the reply into the DOM as HTML, a reply containing a script tag or an event handler can run in the user's browser.

An injected document could make the model output <img src=x onerror=...>. If you render it with innerHTML (or dangerouslySetInnerHTML), that script runs. Render as text, or sanitise Markdown with a safe renderer, and set a content security policy.

Review the blocked examples, find which rule fires wrongly, and tune it, instead of switching the guardrail off.

Measure the false-positive rate on real good traffic. Options: loosen the threshold, add context to the check, whitelist known safe patterns, or replace a hard block with a warning and human review. Keep a test set of good and bad examples so each change shows both rates.

Propose automatic drafts that a person sends, and allow full automation only for low-risk cases such as replies to known internal senders.

Draft-and-approve keeps most of the time saving: the assistant writes, the user presses send. Later, allow auto-send for narrow cases with rules (known recipient, no attachments, no links, a log and an undo window). Show the product team the leak risk with a demo attack.

Plan a test with poisoned emails, hidden instructions, links and attachments, and try to make the assistant leak data or send mail without approval.

Ask a mix of developers, security staff and outside testers. Track each successful attack, fix it, and keep it as a regression test. Launch only to a small group first, with logging and a kill switch.

I would include: least-privilege tools, injection-aware input handling, output encoding, personal data rules, logging of every tool call, and an evaluation set that includes attack prompts.

Add data-flow questions: what private data can the model see, what untrusted text enters, and what can it send out? If all three are present, require human approval. A short list used in every design review keeps it consistent.

Mix people: the developers who built it, security engineers, and someone outside the team who thinks differently.

Builders know the weak spots, but they also share the same assumptions. Add outside testers or a specialist team before major launches, and run automated attack suites continuously. Give red teamers clear scope and a safe way to report.

code.title: Call a model over HTTP from server code (fake handler)

followUps:
Managed identity gives your app a short-lived token from Azure with no secret to store, leak or rotate.

An API key sits in config or a pipeline variable and can be copied, committed by mistake or stay valid for years. With managed identity on App Service or a container app, DefaultAzureCredential gets a token for the Azure OpenAI or Foundry resource, and access is controlled with a role assignment. It works for Azure-hosted model endpoints; other providers may still need a key, which belongs in Key Vault.

Give them a fake or local endpoint: a stub IChatClient that returns canned replies, or a small mock server, plus a development config.

They set AI:UseFake=true in user secrets and the front end runs against the same API shape without real keys or cost. Real keys stay out of the repository. A shared dev deployment with a low spending limit is a second option.

code.title: Depend on an interface so tests use a fake client

followUps:
Inject a fake IChatClient that returns fixed replies, then assert on what your code does with them and on the messages it sent.

Test the prompt-building (the fake records the messages), the parsing of valid and invalid replies, the retry on error, and the tool-calling loop with a scripted sequence of replies. Real model quality belongs in the evaluation suite, not in unit tests, since a unit test must be fast and repeatable.

Use the provider SDK directly when you need a feature the abstraction does not expose yet, or provider-specific behaviour.

Examples: a brand-new model capability, batch APIs, fine-tuning management, or special caching controls. Isolate that code in one adapter class so the rest of the app is unaffected, and move to the abstraction when it catches up.

code.title: Stream pieces as server-sent events

followUps:
Use server-sent events for one-way text streaming such as a chat reply; use SignalR when you need two-way, many-client or group messaging.

SSE is simple HTTP, works through most proxies, reconnects automatically in browsers and needs no extra package. SignalR adds hubs, groups, fallbacks and server-to-client calls for things like live collaboration. For "stream one answer to one user", SSE or a streamed fetch is usually enough.

Collect the pieces into a buffer while forwarding them, and save the complete text after the stream ends (also on cancel or error).

In the endpoint, append each update to a StringBuilder, and in a finally block store the final reply and the token usage with the conversation id. If the user closes the tab, the CancellationToken fires; decide whether to save the partial text.

code.title: Retry 429 with exponential backoff and jitter

followUps:
Jitter spreads retries over time so many clients do not all retry at the same instant and cause another burst.

If 200 requests are throttled together and all wait exactly 2 seconds, 200 arrive again at second 2 and are throttled again. With a random wait between 0 and 2 seconds they arrive spread out. Also respect the Retry-After header when the provider sends it.

Show a friendly "busy, trying again" state, keep partial progress, and offer a simple fallback instead of a raw error.

Examples: a spinner with a message after 3 seconds, queue the request and notify when done, return a cached or non-AI result (plain search results), or switch to a smaller model. Never show provider error text or keys. Log every throttle so you can raise quotas.

Check how stable the API is, who maintains it, how often it breaks, licence, test and security history, and whether it solves a problem you have today.

Do a small spike (one or two days) on a real use case, wrap it behind your own interface so you can remove it, and pin the version. If breaking changes arrive every month and you only use 10% of it, writing the small part yourself may be cheaper.

Remove it when it blocks you more than it helps: frequent breaking changes, hidden prompts or behaviour you cannot control, hard debugging, or when the platform offers the same feature natively.

Because you wrapped it behind your own interface, removal means replacing one adapter. Track how many hours the team spends fighting the framework compared with the code it saves.

For example, an assistant suggested a method that does not exist in the library version we used. The build caught it, but a similar mistake could have compiled.

I caught problems by compiling, running the tests, reading the library docs for anything unfamiliar, and checking security-sensitive code by hand. Tell this kind of story in your own words: what it got wrong, how you noticed, and what habit you changed after.

I never delegate the final responsibility: security-critical code, secrets, architecture decisions and anything I cannot explain.

I do not paste secrets or customer data into tools that are not approved. I also review the design myself, since an assistant optimises the code in front of it, not the long-term system. It can propose; I decide and own the result.

Ask the author to split it into reviewable pieces, and review the tests, the design and the risky areas first.

A 2,000-line change cannot be understood in one sitting. Ask for several PRs of a few hundred lines, or a walk-through call. Check that the tests pass, read the interfaces and data access, and run the code. If the author cannot explain it, it does not merge.

Use an AI reviewer as an extra reader that comments, but not as the one who approves; a human who understands the change must approve.

AI review finds typos, missing null checks and some bugs, and it saves time on first pass. It misses business rules and context, and it can be wrong with confidence. Accountability stays with people, so approval stays human.

Start by listening to the reasons, then agree on outcomes, not tools: the work must meet the same quality, security and delivery standards.

Ask what they tried and what did not work; their concerns about quality or licensing may be right. Offer an experiment on a small task and compare. Do not force use, but do not let it block team conventions. Use their skill for reviews, which matter more with AI-written code.

Have them write and explain the core logic themselves, and use the tool to review, explain and test, not to produce everything.

Practices: ask juniors to explain every generated line in review, pair programming sessions, tasks done without AI for fundamentals, and asking the tool to quiz or explain rather than answer. Measure learning through their ability to debug and design, not just output.

Start by asking which user problem it solves and how we will measure it, then offer a smaller test or a non-AI alternative.

Show the cost, risk and evidence: "a pilot on one workflow for 4 weeks, success = 20% less handling time". Agree what result would stop the project. Say yes to the goal, and be honest about the method. Respect the stakeholder by bringing data, not just objections.

Usually the problem is outside the model: unclear success measures, poor data, no owner, no integration into daily work, or users who do not trust it.

A summariser can be accurate, yet fail if it sits in a separate tab no one opens. Plan the workflow, the users' training, a feedback button, an owner and a measured goal from the start. Run the pilot with real users, not just a demo.
